Kelme Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Šiaulių apskritis, Lithuania

Not demolished. Kelmė was home to the Great Talmud Torah, a renowned yeshiva of the Musar ethical movement founded in the 19th century by Simhah-Zisl Ziv-Broida — known as the Alter of Kelm — a pupil of the movement's founder, Rabbi Yisrael Salanter; the school became famous throughout the Jewish world and drew students from far beyond Lithuania. The town also produced Zvi Yaakov Oppenheim, a co-founder of the renowned Telz Yeshiva, and Aryeh Leib Frumkin, a founding pioneer of Petah Tikva, one of the earliest modern Zionist settlements in Ottoman Palestine. Kelmė's Jewish community, administratively part of the Keidan district within the Lithuanian Jewish Council (Va'ad Medinath Lita), reached 2,710 people — 69 percent of the town — by 1897. German forces began persecuting the community immediately after entering on June 26, 1941, and most of Kelmė's Jews were murdered in mass executions that July and August, totaling around 2,000 victims, carried out by both Lithuanian auxiliary police and German soldiers. This cemetery dates to the 18th century; a bakery was built on its edge during the Soviet period, but the site was otherwise left undisturbed.
